_comment: Per-artwork creation-date corrections, keyed by objectKey (folder/filename, NFC-normalised). Applied by build-data.mjs after extractYear, so it overrides whatever normalize-metadata.mjs derived. This file exists because the derived year is not durable: normalize-metadata.mjs recomputes entry.year on every run, and fetch-wikimedia-metadata.mjs spawns it after every scrape, so a correction written into a sidecar is reverted by the next ingest. Corrections belong here instead. 'year' is the integer the catalogue sorts and shelves by; 'dateString' is how the source words it, shown on the detail page. Every entry cites the page it came from in _why. Never enter a date you have not read on Commons, Wikidata, or the holding institution's own catalogue. Regenerate data with 'pnpm assets:build-data' after editing.

_why.collection-of-beauty/Annibale_Carracci_S: The Commons wikitext has date = {{other date|century|16}} — literally '16th century' and nothing more — which the pipeline collapsed to the century midpoint 1550, five years before Carracci was born (1560). The file page names the National Gallery of Art as the institution and gives the print as an engraving, 31 x 35.1 cm. The NGA's own object record for that print (object 55841, also reachable as art-object-page.55841.html) is titled 'Susanna and the Elders, c. 1590/1595', an etching and engraving with plate 34.7 x 31.2 cm, matching the Commons dimensions. NGA's server returns 403 to direct fetches, so I read the record through its indexed page title and description rather than the live page — hence medium confidence. The date is a genuine bracket, not a single year; 1590 is the best single integer. Source: https://www.nga.gov/artworks/55841-susanna-and-elders. Independently re-checked: SURVIVES, but on a substituted source. The cited https://www.nga.gov/artworks/55841-susanna-and-elders returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch, as does https://www.nga.gov/collection/art-object-page.55841.html and api.nga.gov — so the researcher's own reading of it (self-described as via indexed page title, not the live page) is not something I could reproduce, and on the strict rule that would be a rejection. I therefore re-verified independently: the National Gallery of Art's own catalogue record republished on Google Arts & Culture loads and states 'Susanna and the Elders', Annibale Carracci, date created 1590/1595, etching and engraving on laid paper, National Gallery of Art, Washington DC. I read that page directly. Corroborating (search result titles only, not read): NGA's page for object 55841 is titled 'Susanna and the Elders, c. 1590/1595', and a second NGA impression (object 140823) carries the same c. 1590/1595 date. I independently confirmed the Commons file page: its Artwork date field says literally '16th century' and nothing more, institution National Gallery of Art, engraving, 35.1 x 31 cm. Note a version caveat the researcher did not flag: the GA&C impression's sheet is 31.8 x 31.1 cm, which does not match the Commons file's 35.1 x 31 cm, so the Commons scan is probably NGA's other impression (140823) rather than 55841 — but both are impressions of the same Carracci print and both carry the same 1590/1595 bracket, so the date is unaffected. Lifespan check: Carracci 1560-1609, so 1590/1595 is plausible and the catalogue's current 1550 is impossible (ten years before his birth). The date is a genuine bracket, so 'imprecise' with 1590 as the representative integer is the right call.
_why.collection-of-beauty/Jupiter_and_Juno_An: The Commons file page carries no Artwork date for the fresco at all — its date field is "15 December 2022", the day photographer Aleksandr Sur took and uploaded the image, and there is no Wikidata item for the artwork. The catalogue's 1602 was mined from the uploader's caption, which is not an authoritative source. Wikipedia's Farnese Gallery and The Loves of the Gods articles both date the ceiling cycle only as begun 1597 and "not entirely finished until 1608", and neither assigns a date to the individual Jupiter and Juno panel; other Commons copies of the same fresco are titled 1597. Sources disagree (1597 / 1597-1600 / 1602) and none is authoritative for this panel, so I am leaving the year at 1602 — it sits inside the documented cycle window — rather than substituting an equally unsourced number. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farnese_Gallery. Independently re-checked: SURVIVES, narrowly, because it changes nothing. I checked both pages. The Commons file page's date is the photograph (uploaded 15 December 2022, digitised 11 December 2022); the only occurrence of 1602 anywhere is the uploader's free-text caption "Jupiter and Juno (1602), Palazzo Farnese", which is not an authoritative source — and the local record's description is that same caption string, so the catalogue's 1602 is caption-derived, exactly as the researcher says. The cited Wikipedia article states the cycle was "Painted between 1597 and 1608" and that work started 1597 and was "not entirely finished until 1608"; it assigns no date to the individual Jupiter and Juno panel. So the cited range is real and 1602 falls inside it, but 1602 itself is unsourced. I accept the proposal only on the grounds that it leaves the existing year untouched; had it proposed moving to 1597 or any other specific year on this evidence I would have rejected it.

Institution and accession (Palace on the Water / Lazienki, LKr 890) match. _why.collection-of-beauty/Carl_Spitzweg_-_Im_: Raw wikitext of the Commons {{Art photo}} template: "|date = {{circa|1848}}", "|institution = {{institution:Private collection}}", "|title = {{title|en=The garret|lang=de|Im Dachstübchen / die Dachstube}}", plus DEFAULTSORT "Spitzweg; Garret 2 1848; Private collection" and [[Category:1840s landscape paintings from Germany]]. So the file page's own date field says circa 1848 while its FILENAME says "(v.1849)" — the pipeline took the filename. The template field outranks the filename, but the value is explicitly circa, and because the work is in a private collection there is no institutional catalogue entry to arbitrate; a web search surfaced both "vers 1849" and a 1848–1870 range for a similarly-titled Spitzweg garret picture, none from a museum record I could read. Best available single year is 1848, but the honest reading is c. 1848–1849, and leaving 1849 in place would not be a factual error. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Carl_Spitzweg_-_Im_Dachst%C3%BCbchen_(v.1849).jpg. Independently re-checked: SURVIVES, narrowly. I read the Commons raw wikitext myself and the claim checks out verbatim: the {{Art photo}} template carries "|date = {{circa|1848}}", "|artist = {{Creator:Carl Spitzweg}}", "|title = {{title|en=The garret|lang=de|Im Dachstübchen / die Dachstube}}", "|institution = {{institution:Private collection}}", plus DEFAULTSORT "Spitzweg; Garret 2 1848; Private collection" and [[Category:1840s landscape paintings from Germany]]. The date field is on this file page for this image, so there is no cross-work confusion risk. Our record has year_source "filename" and artist mis-recorded as the photographer "Jean-Marc Pascolo" — the pipeline read "(v.1849)" out of the filename and never consulted the template. Spitzweg 1808-1885, so 1848 is well inside his lifespan. Two caveats keep confidence low: the field is explicitly circa, and with the work in a private collection there is no institutional catalogue to arbitrate 1848 vs 1849. The 1-year delta means the existing 1849 is not a factual error; adopting 1848 merely aligns the catalogue with the only stated source. Either is defensible.

Monet lived at Vétheuil 1878-1881, which corroborates 1880. Source: https://southamptoncityartgallery.com/object/sotag-1975183/. Independently re-checked: SURVIVES, triple-confirmed. (2) The Commons raw wikitext gives |date = {{other date|century|19}}, |wikidata = Q90598726, |source = https://www.southamptoncityartgallery.com/object/sotag-1975183/ — so the file page itself points at exactly this record, ruling out the wrong-version risk. (3) Wikidata Q90598726 ("The Church at Vétheuil") carries P571 = +1880-01-01, precision 9 (year), P170 = Q296 (Monet), P195 = Q7569107 (Southampton City Art Gallery), P217 = "183/1975" — the same inventory number in the gallery's own inverted form. Monet painted the Vétheuil church repeatedly, but accession + collection + the source link tie this file to this record. The current 1850 is the century-precision QS marker read as a literal year, ten years before Monet was born.
_why.collection-of-beauty/Cornelis_de_Vos_-_E: The Commons Artwork template says only '17th century' (the QS string +1650-00-00/7 is a century-precision encoding, which is exactly where the current 1650 came from - it is a rounding artifact, not an assertion). Identity is pinned by inventory number P001860 on both Wikidata and the Prado record, so this is not a different Triumph of Bacchus (the Prado holds several under that title). 1636-1638 sits inside de Vos's life (c. 1584/85-1651) and 1637 is the true midpoint of the stated range. The current 1650 is a century-precision rounding artifact: the sidecar's date_created literally reads '17 th century date QS:P571,+1650-00-00T00:00:00Z/7' with year_source 'era_phrase'. Both values fall in the same Baroque era band, so no floor moves.
_why.collection-of-beauty/Dong_Yuan_Mountain_: The Commons Artwork template date field reads "10th century" with the structured qualifier "date QS:P,+950-00-00T00:00:00Z/7" (century precision), institution National Palace Museum, Taipei, attributed to Dong Yuan (d. 962). The French description on the same page says "milieu du Xe s." The same page also records the scholarly caveat that the attribution to Dong Yuan is stylistic and that the surviving scroll was probably actually executed during the Yuan dynasty (1279–1368). So 950 is the correct reading of the catalogued date, but it is a century-precision placeholder for a work whose real date is disputed — it should not be presented as a firm year. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dong_Yuan_Mountain_Hall.jpg. Independently re-checked: SURVIVES. I fetched the cited Commons page: the Artwork template's date field is "10th century" with the structured qualifier "date QS:P,+950-00-00T00:00:00Z/7" (century precision), artist Dong Yuan (d. 962), institution National Palace Museum, Taipei. The researcher's caveat is also on the page and I confirmed it: the mounted inscription paper attributes the work to Dong Yuan of the Five Dynasties, but the page records that the scroll "was actually done in the Yuan dynasty (1279-1368)" while reflecting his style, and that it bears neither seal nor signature. The sidecar already holds year 950 and date_created "10 th century date QS:P,+950-00-00T00:00:00Z/7", so no integer changes. 950 is the correct reading of the catalogued century-precision date and is consistent with Dong Yuan's lifespan; confidence is medium only because the primary source itself flags the dating as disputed, so 950 must be shown as a century placeholder rather than a firm year.
